content: Astrochemistry is the scientific study of chemical elements and compounds that exist in outer space, typically on scales larger than our Solar System. This field focuses particularly on molecular gas clouds and investigates the processes of their formation, interaction, and destruction. It represents an interdisciplinary overlap between the fields of astronomy and chemistry. On the scale of the Solar System, the study of chemical elements is more commonly referred to as cosmochemistry. Astrochemistry employs telescopes to measure various properties of celestial bodies, such as their temperature and chemical composition. For example, it examines the characteristics of stars or interstellar clouds. The unique spectral signatures of molecules, which are revealed in their spectra, allow scientists to identify and study these molecules. However, there are significant limitations in these measurements. Electromagnetic interference can hinder observations, and the chemical properties of certain molecules pose additional challenges. For instance, molecular hydrogen (H₂), the most abundant molecule in the universe, lacks a dipole moment and cannot be detected using radio telescopes. In contrast, carbon monoxide (CO), which has a strong electric dipole moment, is much easier to detect via radio waves. To date, over a hundred molecules, including radicals and ions, have been identified in space. These include a wide variety of organic compounds such as alcohols, acids, aldehydes, and ketones. There have even been claims of detecting interstellar glycine, the simplest amino acid, though these claims remain controversial. Research is ongoing to understand how interstellar and circumstellar molecules form and interact. This research has profound implications for understanding the origins of life on Earth. As a result, molecules and molecular ions that are unstable on Earth can be highly abundant in space. A notable example is the H₃⁺ ion. Astrochemistry also intersects with astrophysics and nuclear physics, particularly in the study of nuclear reactions within stars. These reactions drive stellar evolution and the formation of successive generations of stars. Nuclear reactions in stars are responsible for producing all naturally occurring chemical elements. As stellar generations progress, the mass of newly formed elements increases. For example, first-generation stars primarily use hydrogen as a fuel source, converting it into helium through nuclear fusion. Hydrogen, the most abundant element in the universe, serves as the fundamental building block for all other elements due to its simple nucleus, which contains only one proton. The immense gravitational forces at the core of a star generate extreme heat and pressure, triggering nuclear fusion. This process fuses lighter nuclei to form heavier elements. Elements such as lithium, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen are synthesized through stellar fusion. Heavier elements, including iron and lead, are also formed in later stages of stellar evolution.
